doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Feeling fortunate: career and union pension
summary: Wilder says he has been a fortunate musician and has an AFM pension, unlike the Ellington, Herman and Basie bandsmen.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: You must look at your career and be pretty happy.

Yeah, I am. I’ve been one of the most fortunate musicians I guess in the country. Most of the things I did I did with people I enjoyed doing them with. Most of the music I was involved with I got great enjoyment out of, and I still do. Like the guys who we were here with the other night. I mean how can you go someplace, as an employee, and have that much fun? It’s unreal.

Where is the state of — I’m not sure how to ask this question, but over the years, has the way the business been set up provided you with some kind of retirement? For twenty years from now when you stop playing.

Well I get a pension from the Federation, the American Federation of Musicians. And having worked in the theater and done those jobs from which money was extracted for your pension, I’m in pretty good shape. Unfortunately when you look back and you look at Duke Ellington’s band, Woody Herman’s band, Count Basie’s band, those fellas had absolutely nothing going into a pension fund. They had nothing going in there, so that when they finished playing, it was like if they hadn’t saved any money on their own, that was it. When the earning thing stopped, that was the end of their ability to earn money, there was nothing left. And of course when you’re on the road with a band, and especially © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -18-
when you’re younger, we all had the idea that this goes on forever. I mean you never look into the future, you don’t think that way, you have no reason to. But I’m one of the fortunate guys, really.
